item.title: Microsoft Unveils New Copilot Super App for Work
item.description:
Microsoft Unveils New Copilot Super App for Work

Microsoft has officially unveiled a redesigned Copilot “super app” that bundles chat, coding, and AI agents into a single interface designed for work.

🔍 Overview

The new Copilot app serves as the default landing experience for users and is organized into three primary tabs:

Tab Description
Home Combines Copilot Chat and Cowork; includes a “Today” personalized dashboard for emails, meeting requests, and Teams threads.
Code Allows users to create and share apps, trackers, dashboards, or automations as cloud-hosted internal apps.
Autopilot A cloud-based personal AI assistant (formerly known as Scout) that acts as a “digital teammate.”

🧩 How it works

The Code Tab

  • Powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot.
  • Runs in a sandboxed environment and can be hosted securely within a tenant.

Autopilot Agents

  • Operates on its own cloud computer instance with its own identity, memory, computer, and workspace.
  • Built on Microsoft IQ to understand organizational workflows.
  • Can be @mentioned in Teams, Outlook, chats, channels, and documents.
  • Capable of watching Teams channels, running recurring work tasks, or handling follow-ups.

⚙️ Key details

Microsoft is introducing a hybrid billing model for the service:

  • User Subscription License: Provides access to Copilot in Chat, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams.
  • Usage-Based Billing: Applies to Cowork, Code, and Autopilot, including long-running agentic capabilities or the use of models such as Astra and Fable.
  • Management: Microsoft uses an auto model picker for tasks; IT admins can use a new “FinOps for AI” tool to manage spend.

🚀 Availability

  • Home and Code tabs: Rolling out to the Frontier program for early access in the coming weeks.
  • Autopilot: Entering private preview later this month.
  • Code (Premium/Pro): Preview available for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.

💡 Why it matters

Microsoft aims for the new Copilot to be as influential as Office, with Jared Spataro, chief marketing officer of AI at work at Microsoft, stating, “Just as Office defined work for the PC era, the new Copilot is built to define it for the AI era.”

#Microsoft #Copilot #AIagents #EnterpriseAI #Productivity

Source: Microsoft thinks its new Copilot ‘super app’ will be as influential as Office

item.title: Microsoft Announces Eight Updates to Microsoft 365 Admin Center Collaboration Tools
item.description:
Microsoft Announces Eight Updates to Microsoft 365 Admin Center Collaboration Tools

Microsoft has introduced eight new updates to the Microsoft 365 Admin Center focused on its collaboration tools suite.

⚙️ Key details

The following features and updates have been added to Microsoft 365 collaboration tools:

Feature Description
SharePoint News Ability to cross-post to Viva Engage
Teams Workflows A new form trigger
Viva Engage Reduced email notifications
Teams Lobby visibility updates
PowerPoint Copilot Two new skills
Teams Centralized channel notification settings
Viva Engage Entra permission requirements
Teams Ability to temporarily pause notifications

item.title: Microsoft Argues Copilot Chat Logs Show Rare Copyright Regurgitation in Lawsuit
item.description:
Microsoft Argues Copilot Chat Logs Show Rare Copyright Regurgitation in Lawsuit

Microsoft has filed new legal documents arguing that its Copilot chatbot rarely reproduces full sentences from news articles or books, asserting that virtually no users are obtaining copyrighted publisher content through the tool.

⚖️ Legal arguments and fair use

Microsoft submitted its filing on Friday as it argues for the judge to issue a summary judgment, which would end the case at an early stage. The company argues that the data bolsters its case that using copyrighted content for AI training datasets should be considered fair use. While systems like Copilot rely on using copyrighted material, Microsoft says the resulting systems are used for significantly different purposes than the original. The fact that they sometimes reproduce sections of text, the company concludes, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.”

📊 Analysis of chat logs

As part of the lawsuit’s discovery, Microsoft provided 8.2 million Copilot chat logs to an expert hired by news publishers. The logs were specifically chosen because they hit on keywords implicating the use of the publishers’ websites, making them the most likely to contain the plaintiffs’ works. According to Microsoft, the resulting analysis shows very low rates of reproduction:

  • Fewer than 1 percent of the more than 8 million chat logs regurgitated at least 16 words.
  • A total of 59,545 logs contained at least 16 words in common with news content used to ground the AI model.
  • An expert for the Center for Investigative Reporting (CIR) found 51 instances of “substantial overlap” with CIR work in the dataset.
  • An expert in the authors’ suit found that the 8.2 million conversations had only 24 responses containing at least 30 matching words.
  • Only 10 of the 212 books evaluated had any matches.

🔍 Case background

The filings were made as part of a legal battle brought by publishers and authors against Microsoft and OpenAI. The plaintiffs claim the companies built products on their works and now compete with them directly, in part by regurgitating copyrighted content.

To streamline the process, the news publishers’ and book authors’ claims were consolidated under one judge, despite objections from the plaintiffs. In addition, the Trump administration filed a statement of interest in the New York Times case this week, supporting OpenAI. If the judge sides with the publishers and authors, the legal battle will continue in court.

The New York Times, CIR, and the Authors Guild did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

#Microsoft #Copilot #Copyright #ArtificialIntelligence

Source: Microsoft says virtually nobody was grabbing NYT articles through its chatbot
